title: Medicine Ball Chest Pass
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball chest pass against a wall: setup, steps, form cues and the mistakes that steal power from the throw.
content:
The medicine ball chest pass is an explosive push: you throw the ball from your chest into a wall and catch it on the rebound. Because you let go of the ball, you can push as fast as possible without having to brake at the end, which is the part a regular push-up or bench press never trains.

It suits beginners who want to build upper-body power, and it works as a warm-up primer before a push workout. All you need is a ball and a solid wall.
steps: Stand about one metre (3–4 ft) from a solid wall with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Hold the ball at chest height with your hands on its sides and your thumbs pointing up behind it.
Brace your core and push the ball hard off your chest, straightening your arms toward the wall at chest height.
Catch the rebound with soft elbows and let the ball travel back to your chest.
Reset your grip and posture, then throw again.
cues: Throw through the wall, not at it.
Keep your elbows slightly below shoulder height.
Finish each throw with your arms fully straight and your thumbs turned down.
mistakes: Flaring the elbows out wide: keep them tucked at roughly 45 degrees to protect the shoulders.
Leaning back to throw: stay tall with ribs down so the push comes from your chest and arms.
Using a ball that is too heavy: if the ball drops before reaching the wall, go lighter.

title: Medicine Ball Slam
excerpt: How to do a medicine ball slam with good form: the right ball to use, step-by-step technique, form cues and common mistakes.
content:
The medicine ball slam takes the ball from overhead and drives it into the floor as hard as you can. It trains your lats, core and shoulders to produce force together, and a few sets raise your heart rate quickly, which is why slams show up in both power and conditioning workouts.

Use a slam ball, a soft-shelled ball made to absorb impact. A standard rubber medicine ball can bounce straight back up toward your face.
steps: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding the ball at your waist with both hands.
Lift the ball overhead, rising onto the balls of your feet and reaching your arms long.
Pull the ball down hard and slam it into the floor just in front of your feet, hinging at the hips as you follow through.
Bend your knees and pick the ball up with a flat back.
Stand tall and go straight into the next rep.
cues: Reach tall at the top: the bigger the stretch, the harder the slam.
Slam with your whole body, crunching your abs as the ball comes down.
Exhale sharply on every slam.
mistakes: Throwing with the arms only: drive the ball down by pulling your trunk forward, not just bending your elbows.
Rounding the back to pick up the ball: squat down to it and keep your chest up.
Slamming a bouncy ball: use a non-bouncing slam ball so it stays on the floor.

title: Wall Ball
excerpt: How to do wall balls: squat, drive and throw the medicine ball to a target. Step-by-step technique, form cues and common mistakes.
content:
A wall ball combines a full squat with an upward throw to a target on the wall. You catch the ball as it falls and drop straight into the next squat, so your legs, shoulders and lungs all work at once.

Wall balls are a staple of conditioning workouts. The squat has to be solid before you add the throw, so they suit people who can already squat to parallel without pain.
steps: Stand an arm's length from a wall, feet slightly wider than hip-width, holding the ball at your chest with your elbows under it.
Pick a target spot on the wall a few feet above your head.
Squat down until your hips drop to at least knee height, keeping your chest up.
Drive up hard through your heels and use that momentum to throw the ball to the target.
Catch the ball at chest height and sink straight into the next squat.
cues: Let your legs throw the ball; your arms only finish the job.
Keep your elbows under the ball, not flared out.
Catch high and ride the ball down into the squat.
mistakes: Squatting too shallow: hit the same depth every rep or the legs do little of the work.
Standing too far from the wall: the ball comes back at an angle and pulls you forward.
Pausing between reps: absorb the catch and flow into the squat to keep the rhythm.

title: Medicine Ball Russian Twist
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball Russian twist: seated rotation steps, how to make it easier or harder, and the mistakes that strain your lower back.
content:
The medicine ball Russian twist is a seated rotation: you lean back, hold the ball in front of you and turn it from side to side. Your obliques do most of the work, while the rest of your core holds you in the leaned-back position.

Keeping your heels on the floor makes it beginner-friendly. Lifting your feet and using a heavier ball are the two ways to progress it.
steps: Sit on the floor with your knees bent and your heels on the ground.
Hold the ball at chest height and lean back until you feel your abs switch on, keeping your back straight.
Rotate your shoulders to one side and bring the ball beside your hip.
Turn back through the middle and rotate to the other side.
Count one rep per side.
cues: Turn your shoulders, not just your arms.
Keep your chest tall; a rounded back takes the work off your obliques.
Move at a controlled pace you could stop at any point.
mistakes: Rounding the lower back: lean back less and sit tall.
Swinging the ball with the arms: the ball should move because your torso turns.
Lifting the feet too early: keep your heels down until 10 controlled reps per side feel easy.

title: Medicine Ball Overhead Throw
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball overhead throw: a soccer-style throw that trains your lats, abs and triceps to produce power. Steps, cues and mistakes.
content:
The medicine ball overhead throw follows the same movement as a soccer throw-in. You take the ball behind your head and launch it forward to a wall or partner. It trains the lats, abs and triceps to fire together and fast.

It's a good pick for anyone who wants more power for overhead sports such as volleyball, tennis or cricket bowling. Use a light ball; speed matters more than load here.
steps: Stand facing a wall or partner, about 2–3 metres (7–10 ft) away, in a split stance.
Hold the ball with both hands and take it overhead and slightly behind your head.
Brace your abs, then throw the ball forward hard, snapping your arms over the top.
Let your back foot step through if you need to.
Catch or collect the ball and reset before the next throw.
cues: Start the throw from your abs and lats, then finish with your arms.
Keep the ball behind your head only as far as your shoulders move comfortably.
Every rep is a full-effort throw; stop the set when the speed drops.
mistakes: Arching the lower back to load the throw: keep your ribs down and brace first.
Using a heavy ball: a slow throw trains strength, not power. Go lighter.
Throwing with bent elbows only: reach long overhead so the whole body adds to the throw.

title: Medicine Ball Backward Throw
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball backward overhead throw: a hip-driven power throw. Space needed, step-by-step technique, cues and mistakes.
content:
The medicine ball backward throw, often called the scoop toss, swings the ball between your legs and launches it up and backward over your head. The power comes from snapping your hips forward, the same action as a jump or a kettlebell swing.

You need open space behind you, ideally outdoors or in a sports hall, and nothing within 10 metres of where the ball lands. Learn the hip hinge first; this throw is not a starting point for complete beginners.
steps: Stand with your back to an open space, feet shoulder-width apart, holding the ball at waist height with straight arms.
Hinge at the hips and bend your knees, bringing the ball down between your legs.
Drive your hips forward and extend your knees explosively, swinging the ball up with straight arms.
Release the ball overhead and behind you as your body reaches full extension, finishing up on your toes.
Walk to the ball, collect it and reset.
cues: Jump with the ball: the throw comes from your legs and hips.
Keep your arms straight; they guide the ball, they don't lift it.
Release when your body is fully straight, not before.
mistakes: Squatting instead of hinging: push your hips back so your hamstrings load before the throw.
Throwing with bent arms: straight arms let the hip drive transfer into the ball.
Throwing indoors near walls or people: always check the landing area first.

title: Medicine Ball Rotational Throw
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball rotational throw against a wall: side-on stance, hip-led rotation, form cues and common mistakes.
content:
The medicine ball rotational throw has you stand side-on to a wall, turn away and then rotate hard to throw the ball into it. It trains your hips and obliques to produce rotational power, the movement behind swinging a bat, racket or golf club.

It's the natural next step once the Russian twist feels easy, because it asks your core to rotate fast instead of slowly.
steps: Stand side-on to a solid wall, about one metre away, feet slightly wider than shoulder-width.
Hold the ball at hip height with both hands and turn away from the wall, shifting weight onto your back leg.
Drive your back hip toward the wall and let your torso and arms follow, throwing the ball into the wall.
Catch the rebound, turn away again and repeat.
Finish all reps on one side, then switch.
cues: Hips first, then shoulders, then arms.
Pivot on the back foot as you throw, like squashing a bug under your heel.
Keep a slight bend in your elbows so the force comes from rotation.
mistakes: Throwing with the arms: if your hips don't turn, the throw is all shoulders.
Twisting from the lower back: let the hips and back foot turn so the spine isn't forced.
Doing only your strong side: match the reps on both sides.

title: Medicine Ball Lying Leg Raise
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball lying leg raise: ball between the feet, controlled lowering, and how to keep your lower back on the floor.
content:
The medicine ball lying leg raise is a standard leg raise with a ball squeezed between your feet. The extra weight at the end of your legs makes your abs work harder to keep your pelvis still while your legs lower.

The test is whether your lower back stays flat on the floor. If it lifts, the ball is too heavy or your legs are going too low.
steps: Lie on your back with your arms by your sides, palms down, and squeeze a light ball between your feet.
Press your lower back into the floor and lift your straight legs until they point at the ceiling.
Slowly lower your legs as far as you can while your lower back stays flat.
Stop just above the floor, or higher if your back starts to lift.
Raise your legs back up and repeat.
cues: Lower back glued to the floor the whole set.
Take three seconds to lower, one to lift.
Squeeze the ball so your legs move as one unit.
mistakes: Lower back arching off the floor: shorten the range or bend your knees slightly.
Dropping the legs fast: control the lowering phase, that's where the abs work hardest.
Using a heavy ball: start with the lightest one you have.

title: Medicine Ball Dead Bug
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball dead bug: a beginner core exercise that trains your abs to hold your spine still while your arms and legs move.
content:
The medicine ball dead bug is a back-friendly core exercise. You lie on your back holding a ball above your chest and slowly extend your legs while your abs keep your lower back still. Holding the ball keeps your arms working and your upper body stable.

It's one of the safest ways for a beginner to build core control before moving on to leg raises or rotational work.
steps: Lie on your back holding the ball with straight arms above your chest.
Lift your legs so your knees are bent at 90 degrees, stacked over your hips.
Press your lower back into the floor and brace your abs.
Slowly straighten one leg, lowering the heel toward the floor without touching it.
Bring it back to the start and repeat with the other leg.
cues: Breathe out slowly as the leg extends.
Keep the ball still over your chest; it shouldn't drift.
Move slowly enough that your lower back never lifts.
mistakes: Arching the lower back: keep the leg higher until your abs can hold the position.
Holding your breath: exhale through each rep so you can brace properly.
Rushing the reps: count two seconds out, two seconds back.

title: Medicine Ball Close-Grip Push-Up
excerpt: How to do a push-up with both hands on a medicine ball: setup, steps, a knee version for beginners, and the mistakes that strain your wrists.
content:
The medicine ball close-grip push-up puts both hands on top of a ball under your chest. The narrow hand position shifts more of the work to your triceps and inner chest, and balancing on the ball makes your shoulders and core work harder than in a floor push-up.

You need to manage 10 regular push-ups with good form first. If you can't yet, do this version from your knees.
steps: Place a firm, non-rolling medicine ball on the floor and put both hands on top of it, fingers spread down its sides.
Walk your feet back into a push-up position with your body in a straight line from head to heels.
Bend your elbows and lower your chest toward the ball, keeping your elbows close to your sides.
Push back up until your arms are straight.
Keep your hips level with your shoulders throughout.
cues: Squeeze the ball with your hands to keep it still.
Elbows brush your ribs on the way down.
For the knee version, keep a straight line from knees to head.
mistakes: Hips sagging: brace your abs and squeeze your glutes.
Elbows flaring out: keep them tucked so your triceps share the load.
Using a soft or bouncy ball: a firm ball with a textured surface is less likely to roll.

title: Medicine Ball Crunch
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball crunch: holding a ball to load a basic crunch, step-by-step technique, form cues and common mistakes.
content:
The medicine ball crunch is a regular crunch with a ball held at your chest or above it. The extra load lets you train your abs harder without simply adding more and more reps.

Holding the ball close to your chest is the easiest version. Pressing it straight up toward the ceiling makes the same crunch harder.
steps: Lie on your back with your knees bent and your feet flat on the floor.
Hold the ball against your chest, or press it straight up above your chest for a harder version.
Breathe out and curl your head, shoulders and upper back off the floor.
Pause for a second at the top with your abs squeezed.
Lower slowly back down and repeat.
cues: Curl your ribs toward your hips; don't sit all the way up.
Keep a fist-sized gap between your chin and chest.
Lower down slower than you came up.
mistakes: Pulling with the neck: the ball stays still relative to your chest and your abs do the lifting.
Coming up too far: once your lower back leaves the floor, your hip flexors take over.
Bouncing off the floor: pause briefly at the bottom of each rep.

title: Medicine Ball Woodchop Squat
excerpt: How to do the medicine ball woodchop squat: a diagonal low-to-high rotation that trains your legs and obliques together. Steps, cues, mistakes.
content:
The medicine ball woodchop squat moves the ball diagonally from outside one knee to above the opposite shoulder as you stand up from a squat. It ties your legs and core together in a rotating pattern similar to lifting a bag into a car.

It's a good beginner introduction to rotational training because you stay in control the whole time; nothing is thrown.
steps: Stand with your feet slightly wider than shoulder-width, holding the ball with both hands.
Squat down and rotate, bringing the ball to the outside of your right knee.
Stand up and turn your torso to the left, lifting the ball diagonally across your body to above your left shoulder.
Reverse the movement under control back to the bottom position.
Do all reps on one side, then switch.
cues: Pivot your back foot as you rotate up.
Keep your arms nearly straight so the ball travels in a long arc.
Lead with your chest, not your hands.
mistakes: Rounding the back at the bottom: squat lower rather than bending forward.
Knees caving in at the bottom: push them out over your toes.
Moving too fast: this is a controlled chop, not a throw.
